title_en: Phase Transitions in Heavy-Tailed Mean Estimation under $\ell_p$ Norms
abstract_en: We study the problem of estimating the mean of a random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ under $\ell_p$ norms, assuming only the existence of a covariance matrix. In the Euclidean norm, the sample mean is already optimal in expectation, and robust estimators are usually needed only to obtain high-probability tails. Our results show that this picture changes for $\ell_p$ norms with $p>2$: robustification is already necessary even for the expected risk. We prove that the minimax risk exhibits a sharp phase transition, controlled by the interaction between the sample size $n$, the dimension $d$, and the norm parameter $p$. In the large-sample regime, the classical Gaussian rate remains achievable. In the complementary regime, heavy-tailed distributions create a genuinely non-Gaussian obstruction. Furthermore we show that the simple estimator: coordinate-wise median of means whose number of buckets chosen according to the geometry of the loss, optimally tracks this phase transition in its expected risk minimax. We also show that natural projection-based median-of-means estimators for general norms, despite achieving the optimal confidence trade-off relative to the sample-mean benchmark of Lugosi and Mendelson (Probab. Theory Relat. Fields, 2019), can be polynomially suboptimal for $\ell_p$ norms even in the constant-probability regime.

title_en: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
abstract_en: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.

title_en: QA-CMIF:Accurate and Lightweight Cross-Modal Latent Imputation and Fusion for Fault-Tolerant sEMG-Inertial Hand Gesture Recognition
abstract_en: Fusing surface electromyography (sEMG) with inertial measurements is widely used for myoelectric prosthesis control and wearable human-machine interfaces. In daily wear, however, socket micro-displacement, electrode lift-off, and wire failures often corrupt an unknown subset of sEMG channels through burst artifacts, lift-off shocks, or open-circuit dropouts. Existing fusion networks mix all channels in the first convolutional layer, so a few corrupted electrodes contaminate the entire latent representation, whereas gate-only attenuation of corrupted channels discards the co-activation cues needed to separate fine-grained gestures. We propose QA-CMIF, a quality-aware cross-modal latent imputation and fusion framework that encodes each sEMG channel independently, scores its reliability with a soft gate, and protects intact channels via a confidence-weighted residual bypass, while a cross-attention imputer repairs degraded channels in latent space using the inertial stream and remaining reliable sEMG channels under a bad-channel alignment loss. title_en: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

title_en: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems
abstract_en: Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions. We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions. Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated. The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.

title_en: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
abstract_en: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

title_en: A plug-in energy-balance freezing module for transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs
abstract_en: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure. We develop a transformer-compatible module that embeds leaf energy-balance physics in freezing-probability forecasts: an energy-balance temperature reference and a learned residual predict leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a temperature-dependent probability cap. We mathematically prove conditional monotonicity and an alarm boundary, and test whether placing the same information in the output pathway or in attention yields different benefits. We evaluated 12 hourly leads at 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons, with and without leaf-sensor inputs. In the 2025-2026 hold-out season without these inputs, our time-token transformer (PET-E) achieved a lead-mean critical success index (CSI) of 0.516 versus 0.478 for fixed-configuration, joint-lead LightGBM, with significant gains at all 12 leads, and the fraction of alarms at observed leaf temperatures of at least 2 degrees C fell from 0.087 to 0.051 relative to the unmodified backbone. Across the hold-out and a retrospective 2024-2025 evaluation, the module reduced Brier scores and warm-surface alarm fractions in both the time-token transformer and iTransformer, with no significant CSI decrease at any lead. At held-out stations without static or leaf-sensor inputs, both module-equipped backbones exceeded LightGBM at all 12 leads (CSI 0.468 and 0.467 versus 0.437). In the time-token backbone, the temperature pathway reduced this alarm fraction in all four settings, whereas the attention prior increased CSI in three. These findings link an explicit temperature-dependent probability cap to improved forecasts and distinguish output-side from attention-based embedding.

title_en: Infrastructure-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Highway Ramp Merging
abstract_en: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion. With recent advances in connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), vehicles can be trained to coordinate for safe and efficient merging. However, in dense traffic, forming an effective observation of the traffic state is challenging. For example, observing only the neighbouring vehicles may lead to locally optimal decisions, while observing the entire traffic can introduce much irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based MARL vehicle control model to address these problems. A roadside infrastructure controller receives the states of all CAVs via vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication and sends control commands back to them. An attention-based observation encoder is designed where each vehicle can filter the relevant vehicle information from the global traffic state. The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.

title_en: Prompt Re-Specification and Target-Mask Availability in Mask-Conditioned Visual Reinforcement Learning for Moving-Platform Landing
abstract_en: Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training. Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM 3 detector changes. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach.

title_en: Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining
abstract_en: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.

title_en: SGIP: Learning Scene-Grounded Interaction Priors for Scene-Aware Human Motion Prediction
abstract_en: Human motion prediction (HMP) aims to forecast future movement from an observed motion sequence, and recent methods have incorporated 3D scene geometry and object semantics to improve long-term plausibility. However, the destination of future motion remains ambiguous in cluttered scenes: the same observed motion can lead to different interaction targets or navigation modes. Existing methods either handle this ambiguity implicitly or rely on auxiliary signals like gaze that are hard to obtain in practice. To address this, we propose SGIP, which explicitly predicts where in the scene future motion will be grounded across both objects and open navigation regions, and uses it to condition future trajectory and full-body pose prediction. This scene-grounded interaction prior is learned via intent distillation: at training time only, a teacher model scores candidate scene regions by combining an LLM prompted with a textual description of the person's intent with geometric motion-scene features. A student model learns to reproduce these scores from only the observed motion and 3D scene, making intent and LLM unnecessary at test time. Across multiple benchmark datasets, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and pose accuracy in a realistic deployment setting where neither gaze nor intent is available at inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework. title_en: GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment
abstract_en: Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). title_en: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
abstract_en: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain.

title_en: U-HamGNN: a universal model for magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned on spin and Hubbard U
abstract_en: The electronic structure of a magnetic crystal depends jointly on its spin configuration and the on-site Hubbard correction U, requiring a separate DFT+U calculation for each combination. We introduce U-HamGNN, an equivariant network that takes these two inputs directly and predicts spin-resolved Hamiltonians across diverse crystal chemistries. A spectral-hybrid optimizer that weights each update direction by how consistently the gradient points along it reaches 8% lower Hamiltonian error than Muon and 26% lower than AdamW in a ten-epoch benchmark. The predicted bands reproduce U-dependent gap opening and altermagnetic spin splitting within the trained window and beyond it; exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls derived from the Hamiltonian agree with DFT+U on a calibration set. This universal model provides a new tool for magnetic research.

title_en: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
abstract_en: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

title_en: KneeFS-Net: A Lightweight Deep Learning Model for Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Assessment with Cross-Domain External Validation
abstract_en: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) grading from radiographs using the Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) scale requires expertise that may be scarce. Without further training or adaptation, the OAI-trained model achieved QWK 0.803, MAE 0.339 and 98.2% within-one-grade accuracy on its hospital cohort, declining to QWK 0.656 and MAE 0.522 on multi-center teleradiology images. title_en: When Zero Is Competitive: A Descriptive Pilot of Transformer and Gate-Graph Surrogates on Random-Angle Quantum Circuits
abstract_en: We examine supervised classical prediction of all one-qubit Z and two-qubit ZZ expectation values on noiseless, layered 4-10-qubit RX/RY/RZ-CNOT circuits. In a 63-cell stratified workload with disjoint circuit-template tests, we evaluate one transformer encoder and gate-dependency graph neural networks against literal-zero and training-derived constant predictors. On the Arm K training labels, 44.89% of scalar targets have absolute magnitude below 0.05. The held-out-template zero predictor has equal-instance mean absolute error 0.193399, and none of the evaluated transformer checkpoints or final graph-network endpoints achieves a lower score. A separate product-state positive control achieves MAE 0.007755 versus 0.514811 for zero, but does not explain the failure on the entangled workload. The difference between zero and a training-fitted mean constant under training MSE is only 0.14%, a descriptive point estimate without uncertainty analysis. The transformer's 815,233-parameter source identity is locally verified; detailed packed-input semantics have not been independently audited. These results constitute a descriptive pilot, not a causal explanation, formal equivalence test, or impossibility claim. Comparable circuits can be regenerated from the workload specification, but exact frozen datasets and model-run evidence remain private.

title_en: The structure of variational autoencoder latent spaces and its consequences for representation and optimization
abstract_en: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used to build low-dimensional representations of scientific data, with the expectation that regularization yields smooth coordinates for interpolation, generation and optimization. However, applications in microscopy reveal domains, narrow transitions and rare-state islands in VAE latent spaces that smoothness alone does not explain. We show that, for prototype data with squared-error reconstruction and an optimal decoder, the latent-space objective has a direct correspondence with the Flory-Huggins theory of a regular solution, and use it to analyze how the objective, posterior distributions and latent dimensionality organize the representation. Data families occupy domains separated by finite-width walls that broaden with increasing regularization until class separation is lost through posterior collapse. Class centroids behave like particles in a harmonic trap: the prior confines them, and structural dissimilarity sets a soft repulsion that determines which classes become neighbors and how far apart they sit, with separations growing only logarithmically with dissimilarity. Rare states can remain unresolved, form small islands, accumulate within walls or develop intervening domains, depending on their frequency and similarity to common states. The posterior covariance can align domains with the latent axes, but axis alignment does not imply separation of physical factors. Rotations can produce rings and encoder cuts that reflect data symmetry, while insufficient dimensionality can lead to suppression, mixing or folding of additional factors. Comparisons with flow models, deep kernel learning (DKL) and hybrid VAE-DKL models show how these structures change when reconstruction and prediction play different roles. We discuss implications for interpreting data, discovering rare states, generating intermediate states and optimizing properties.

title_en: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation
abstract_en: Spatially resolved precipitation retrievals based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) observations and will be used to implement the next operational PMW retrieval algorithm for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. However, the conventional radiative transfer simulations used to extend the retrieval algorithm to the various sensors of the GPM constellation do not provide the spatial coverage required to train CNN-based retrievals. To address this, we introduce a machine-learning-based simulation framework that enables the training of the CNN-based GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm for the full GPM constellation. At the core of this framework is Satformer, a new neural-network architecture that can translate PMW observations between any pair of GPM sensors. The resulting synthetic observations exhibit lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and lead to more accurate precipitation retrievals when used to train GPROF-NN precipitation retrievals. We further demonstrate the applicability of the framework to new instruments by developing GPROF-NN retrievals for the Microwave Imager aboard the Weather System Follow-on Microwave satellite. While GPROF-NN retrievals based on the new simulation framework achieve lower instantaneous retrieval errors and higher correlations compared to independent reference data than conventional retrievals, residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases in the resulting retrievals. The proposed simulation framework provides a key component for extending GPROF-NN to the full GPM constellation as part of the upcoming operational GPROF V08 retrieval algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning-based simulations to support spatially resolved precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations.

title_en: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
abstract_en: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/PPL-TSC.

title_en: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD
abstract_en: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.

title_en: SAGE-VQA: A Training-Free, Self-Evolving Agentic Framework with Grounded Evidence for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
abstract_en: Knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA) aims to combine visual information with external knowledge to answer user questions. Existing methods face two main bottlenecks: visual perception errors can propagate into hallucinations, and generalization across scenarios remains limited. To address these issues, we propose SAGE-VQA (Self-evolving Agent framework with Grounded Evidence), a training-free agentic framework that combines evidence verification with experience evolution. Our key insight is to explore an Evidence-Driven Adaptive Reasoning (EDAR) strategy. It accurately acquires and verifies question-relevant fine-grained visual information. It also extracts and refines reusable experience to support robust reasoning across tasks. Specifically, we design a Co-verified Visual Grounding module that verifies question-relevant visual information and provides grounded evidence for subsequent reasoning. We further introduce a Self-evolving Hierarchical Memory (SHM) mechanism. SHM organizes experiences into declarative and procedural memories based on their nature. These memories can be reused in subsequent reasoning and continually refined through feedback, without updating model parameters. Experimental results show that our method outperforms competing methods based on lightweight open-source vision-language models (VLMs) as well as those based on closed-source VLMs. Moreover, our method can serve as a plug-and-play reasoning framework for existing VLMs without modifying their architectures.

title_en: Attribute or Abstain: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Retrieval on the Low-Resource African Business Web
abstract_en: Retrieval-augmented systems that research companies are judged by how much they find, yet in markets where public evidence is sparse, a confident answer without support costs more than no answer. We introduce AfriBizClaims, a benchmark of 150 company-research queries across six African markets in English, French and Portuguese, including queries about fictitious companies that a correct system must decline. Each claim a system makes is judged against the page it cites by an AI judge, checked against a second AI judge from another model family and against two human annotators, and abstentions are scored against answerability labels. We compare BM25 over a pooled corpus, standard web retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1), all using the same language model. The two simple baselines are well attributed: 98% of their judged claims are supported by the page they cite, and they decline every field of every fictitious company. Counting claims about a company other than the one asked about as errors, the agent pipeline's per-query precision is 68%, and it never answers a question about a named company correctly: it substitutes other firms, including for 5 of the 24 fictitious names, and it is the least stable between runs and the most expensive. In the pipeline we evaluated, more steps between the query and the evidence did not buy more grounded answers. We will release the queries, system outputs, labels and short evidence excerpts.

title_en: LoopSkim: Lossless Multi-Depth Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
abstract_en: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.

title_en: AgenticJevNav: Agentic Object Search and Navigation via Event-Driven Verification
abstract_en: Agentic navigation must maintain goals and adapt actions from incomplete evidence despite execution failures and delayed inference. Jev reviews structured evidence after blocked/failed execution or two consecutive low-progress segments. Version, freshness, and once-only checks govern decision application. title_en: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding and Repairing Risky Fallback in LLM Agents
abstract_en: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.

title_en: Large Language Model-based Optimization for Wireless Communication: A Survey
abstract_en: The growing complexity and dynamism of modern wireless communication frameworks have made real-time optimization essential for efficient resource allocation. Traditional optimization and machine-learning techniques often struggle with generalization, adaptability, stability, and scalability in heterogeneous, time-varying environments. Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools capable of reasoning over structured prompts and generating context-aware decisions in real time without domain-specific retraining. This survey provides a comprehensive review of LLM-driven optimization techniques applied to wireless communication problems such as power control, bandwidth allocation, task offloading, and intelligent surface configuration. We introduce a functional taxonomy of LLM-enabled wireless resource management strategies and analyze the prompt engineering methodologies employed in recent literature. Furthermore, we develop a generalized analytical framework that categorizes LLM-based optimization architectures, including direct solution generation, closed-loop optimization with external verifiers, and representation encoding within trainable neural pipelines. To demonstrate practical applicability, we present representative case studies on LLM-assisted beam prediction for millimeter-wave systems and adaptive wireless resource allocation. Finally, we discuss emerging hybrid AI approaches for wireless networks.

title_en: Let Execution Do the Teaching
abstract_en: Improving a coding model is a sequence of decisions: find the limiting behavior, create useful practice, and determine which attempts deserve reinforcement. We investigate a practical way to make those decisions increasingly repeatable by grounding feedback in execution. Compiler errors and failing tests provide specific contexts for repair practice, while executable checks score the resulting programs. We evaluate the trained models on 26 C++ coding tasks, measuring both initial success and completion after test feedback. The strongest reported post-training configuration achieves 45.2% success in the first test round and 61.5% within two rounds. These results come from an assisted development suite with evolving prompt contracts; the strongest configuration uses four selected evaluation trials and includes six tasks also used in training. The study describes an execution-guided workflow for improving coding models, including how repair tasks are constructed, how program behavior determines rewards, and how the resulting models are evaluated.

title_en: "Don't Leave the Task Unfinished": Persistence-Driven Violations under Quiet Oversight
abstract_en: LLM agents are increasingly given long, multi-step tasks to carry out, with the user reviewing little of what happens in between. Persistence, the tendency to keep working until a task is complete, is installed on purpose to improve performance on long tasks. Long-horizon tasks are typically complex, and the user's instruction can fall short of what the work actually requires, or conflict with the constraints the agent encounters in the task. We study what persistence does on long-horizon operations tasks that cannot be solved without breaking a documented constraint. We find that the agent pursues completion to the point of violating the constraint, and that a critically engaged user lowers the violation rate. Persistence takes violations from 29.2% to 58.3% across four models. Violations stay high wherever oversight goes quiet, whether the user is silent, assenting, or delegating with expressed trust. Only a questioning user, who asks for the basis of each action before allowing the next, brings the rate back to roughly the level measured without persistence. Practitioners should treat high persistence as a setting that carries a safety cost, and should recognize that the cost appears when oversight goes quiet. Safety here is better cast as a property of the human-AI pair than of the model alone. Project page: https://francis21c.github.io/quiet-oversight/

title_en: Illusion of Explainability: A Sanity Check for Spectral Band Attribution in Satellite Time-Series Crop Classification
abstract_en: Attribution methods are commonly validated through convergence across methods and consistency with domain knowledge, yet neither criterion establishes whether identified features are necessary for a task. This limitation is particularly relevant in multispectral remote sensing, where overlapping spectral information makes individual bands potentially substitutable. We investigate this gap in crop-type classification using GradientSHAP, Shapley sampling, and Occlusion on a U-TAE segmentation model trained on Sentinel-2 time series from the PASTIS benchmark. All three methods identify vegetation-sensitive spectral regions consistent with domain knowledge, while Shapley and Occlusion exhibit strong ordering sensitivity in deletion and insertion tests. However, these properties do not reliably predict retraining performance. Aggregate attribution consensus masks substantial per-class disagreement, with pairwise mean Spearman correlations ranging from 0.09 to 0.79. Models retrained from scratch using the five lowest-ranked bands perform comparably to or better than those using the five highest-ranked bands. Furthermore, attribution rankings from an independently trained model with identical configuration and seed identify a different top-five subset that yields better retraining performance. Analysis of all 252 five-band subsets reveals consistently low effective dimensionality (1.35 to 2.62), suggesting substantial spectral redundancy. These findings demonstrate that plausible and apparently faithful attribution rankings do not necessarily identify task-relevant bands for improved retrained performance, highlighting the limitations of band-level feature attribution in spectrally redundant input spaces.

title_en: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
abstract_en: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

title_en: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
abstract_en: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.

title_en: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
abstract_en: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

title_en: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
abstract_en: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

title_en: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
abstract_en: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmea- sured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

title_en: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
abstract_en: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. title_en: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State
abstract_en: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.

title_en: GraphPass: A Study of Graph Neural Networks for Compiler Pass Selection
abstract_en: Compiler pass selection is usually governed by fixed pipelines (-O2, -O3) or hand-written heuristics. We study whether a graph neural network (GNN) over a program's control-flow graph (CFG) can select among a fixed menu of five pass sequences in a single forward pass. GraphPass encodes each CFG with a graph attention (GAT) or graph convolutional (GCN) encoder and classifies it into one of the five sequences. On a synthetic benchmark of 5,000 generated CFGs in five program families, both encoders agree with the benchmark's reference label on about 92% of held-out programs, versus 68.4% for a hand-written rule-based heuristic and 85% for a flat MLP. An edge ablation indicates that this gain comes from per-block processing rather than from CFG edges: a GCN given the same basic-block features with all edges removed scores 95.0%, versus 92.2% with the true CFG. In this benchmark the label is determined by the program family, so the task amounts to family recognition. Real-compiler speedup is not measured. Inference costs O(|V| + |E|) per CFG, measured at 1.7 ms for a typical program and about 0.8 s for a 100,000-block graph on one CPU core.

title_en: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
abstract_en: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.

title_en: The Sense Paradigm for World Models
abstract_en: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.

title_en: When Does Reusing Layers Help Multimodal Embeddings?
abstract_en: We ask whether a compact universal multimodal embedding models can produce better search embeddings by running the same layers again. Looped transformers add computation with nearly unchanged model size, making them an appealing alternative to a larger encoder. Their success in language-model reasoning and recent use for retrieval motivate the idea, but higher retrieval scores alone do not reveal what an extra pass contributes. We study eleven loop designs and training variants on three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture. Our protocol distinguishes whether a model uses its extra pass, whether its image states respond to the query, and whether those updates improve retrieval. We prove that an image placed before the query remains query-independent through repeated layers when information only travels forward. We then open a query-to-image path in three ways, including order-alternating recurrence, which places the query first on the next pass. Each path produces query-sensitive image states. For bidirectional attention and order alternation, freezing later visual updates does not lower accuracy. On all 78 datasets of the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark version 2 (MMEB-V2), a standard added loop loses 0.46 points against its trained control; an intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36. A model pretrained with recurrence gains +4.23 points over its own loop-removed control and benefits from query-conditioned image updates when answering visual questions or locating objects from text.

title_en: Pros4D: Modeling Evolving 4D Worlds in Latent Space for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
abstract_en: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.

title_en: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
abstract_en: Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.

title_en: Logical AI OS: A Training-Free Governance Layer Outside the Model for Instruction Following -- Benefits, Costs, Failures, and the Calibration of the Measuring Instrument Itself
abstract_en: Small language models often fail explicit user requests (length, number of items, format, required or forbidden words, grammatical person, answer language). We measure a training-free governance layer placed outside the model: it reads the requests with rules, checks the answer mechanically, repairs it when a request is not kept, and hands back the original answer when the repair fails. The loop exists in prior work; our contribution is measuring its benefits, costs and failures, and reporting how the measuring instrument itself was calibrated. On four 4-bit Qwen-family models (3B, 7B, 14B, one 7B reasoning model) and 329 Chinese prompts: (1) answers that keep every request the layer read rise significantly (all comparisons p<0.0001), by 34 to 66 of 329 under the corrected checker and 52 to 92 after a length-control fix; a generic redo message brings no significant gain. (2) Exploratory: on 90 repair-triggered prompts, two AI annotators found the layer produced an acceptable answer where the bare model did not more often than the reverse (49:7; 18:12, not significant). (3) Costs: 43-66% more generation time; whole-answer rewriting makes a sizeable share of usable answers unusable. (4) Failures: rule-based reading reaches about 70% and 84% of a two-annotator ceiling on unseen phrasings; unsatisfiable requests make the reasoning model loop; model self-reports are unreliable (18 of 25 "fixed" items were not fixed). (5) Over half of the original checker's "violated" verdicts on structural requests were wrong; after correction the main result holds, and one comparison is downgraded. Conclusions are limited to this Chinese material, the Qwen family and sizes up to 14B. The governance implementation is not released; data, answers, verdicts and the checker are public.

title_en: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix
abstract_en: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.

title_en: Lossless First-Action Menus for Linear-Reward Planning
abstract_en: We study sequential decision making where an agent reserves a minimum menu of initial actions before multi-objective trade-offs are revealed, followed by unrestricted continuation planning once linear reward weights arrive. We prove that a menu preserves the unrestricted optimal return across all linear scalarizations if and only if its reachable continuations cover all vertices of the full feature polytope. This geometric equivalence yields an output-sensitive algorithm that is fixed-parameter tractable in the vertex count, combining scalar backward induction with oracle-based facet identification. On explicitly layered graphs with unit feature increments, menu verification is coNP-complete and synthesis is complete for the second existential level of the polynomial hierarchy, even under additive loss strictly below one. In fixed dimensions two and higher, verification is polynomial whereas synthesis remains NP-complete, while one-dimensional instances admit polynomial-time solutions.

title_en: Read Before You Fit: Text-Derived Constraints for Discovering Differential Equations from Noisy Biological Data
abstract_en: Large language models are increasingly used for scientific equation discovery. However, most existing methods are strongly data-driven and assume sufficiently clean and representative observations. This assumption is problematic in biological systems, where individual-level measurements are often sparse, noisy, heterogeneous, and expensive to obtain. While the underlying mechanisms are extensively described in scientific text, they are not explicitly used for the LLM based modeling of such systems. We introduce P2C, an agentic framework that translates textual descriptions of biological systems into a typed set of formal constraints, and use these constraints to restrict candidate ordinary differential equation (ODE) structures before numerical fitting. P2C consists of five stages: Text2Constraint extraction, ODE discovery, symbolic verification, parameter fitting, and model scoring. We evaluate P2C on four published ODE systems of acute inflammation and immune regulation, under clean and noisy observations. By progressively degrading the numerical evidence, we isolate when textual domain knowledge contributes beyond regression alone. Across the four systems, adding Text2Constraint reduces the worst form error from 1.397 to 0.499 on clean data and from 13.096 to 1.095 for data perturbed with Gaussian noise of $σ=0.1$; P2C also achieves lower form error and trajectory error than several LLM-based baselines over the tested noise range.

title_en: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
abstract_en: Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle. The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

title_en: How Far Is Too Far? Object Recognition Declines Monotonically with Semantic Distance
abstract_en: Vision models are sensitive to object-background context, yet it remains unclear how recognition changes as the semantic distance between objects and backgrounds increases. We introduce ImageNet-OOC1k, a benchmark enabling graded control of object-background relationships along a continuous consensus visual-semantic dissimilarity axis. This formulation reveals a highly consistent monotonic decline in recognition accuracy across 35 models spanning convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, and vision-language models. Using this characterization as a diagnostic probe, a simple spatial re-ranking strategy recovers a subset of these errors and improves in-sample accuracy by up to 5.7 percentage points. title_en: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
abstract_en: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

title_en: Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer
abstract_en: In this paper, we propose a conditional asset pricing transformer (CAP-T) that captures nonlinear interactions among firms through attention to forecast excess returns. In the first stage, a transformer estimates conditional expected returns, and kernel-weighted principal component analysis of its residuals estimates the local factor loading space. Projecting the conditional mean onto this space separates factor risk compensation from conditional mispricing. Then, in the second stage, separate transformers learn these two components, whose predictions are combined to forecast returns. As a result, the proposed framework decomposes returns into conditional mispricing, factor risk compensation, a centered factor component, and an unpredictable innovation. We establish approximation and generalization bounds and characterize how first-stage prediction errors propagate through local factor estimation and component learning, providing statistical guaranties for conditional mispricing, factor loadings, and factor risk premia. Finally, simulations and empirical studies demonstrate the predictive and interpretive benefits of the proposed method.

title_en: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
abstract_en: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. title_en: Fine-Grained RLAIF for Visual Safety: Learning to Zoom into Hazards for Multimodal Safety Alignment
abstract_en: Recent multimodal safety alignment heavily relies on a text-centric paradigm, assuming risks are explicit in language or globally prominent in images. However, real-world hazards are often visually subtle or peripheral, causing existing models to fail due to their reliance on coarse, global visual representations. In this work, we study fine-grained visual safety alignment and introduce a challenging 1,200-sample benchmark across four domains, where hazards necessitate localized inspection. To address this, we propose Fine-Grained RLAIF (FGR), a reinforcement learning framework that casts image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy. FGR employs a decomposed reward design to jointly align three core safety behaviors: (i) where to look via a visual evidence reward, (ii) when to act via a tool-formatting constraint, and (iii) how to reason via visually grounded safety explanations. FGR achieves accuracy ranging from 86.71% to 93.00%, consistently outperforming strong multimodal and agent-based baselines.
