title_en: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
abstract_en: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

title_en: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
abstract_en: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

title_en: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
abstract_en: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

title_en: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
abstract_en: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

title_en: Tensorized Automata: Algebraically Informed Representation Learning for Sequential Decision Making
abstract_en: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it. We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators. AND-OR message passing learns task and state vectors; selected configurations define an event-driven Boolean matrix operator. We prove that initial and successor language coverage make its carrier represent the exact residual after every prefix, with a sufficient capacity bound in terms of reachable configurations. Conjunction and disjunction use the same pipeline. Fidelity and composition audits evaluate copied formulas and learned disjunct assignments. In five-policy-seed XLand experiments with larger training pools, pooled execution-state vectors outperform raw carrier bits and task-blind conditioning across three task pools under two rejection rewards. They achieve 77.3\% success on multi-event tasks and 99.4\% on a four-task stratum with 33--128-state minimal DFAs, using 16 operator slots. LetterWorld results show useful residual conditioning alongside a remaining gap to RAD. These results connect algebraically informed representation learning to compact task execution and useful policy conditioning.

title_en: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
abstract_en: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

title_en: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract_en: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.

title_en: Learning from Duality in Neural Network Field Theories
abstract_en: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields. Level-rank duality connects the charged sectors of the fermionic construction, where explicit neural observables recover conformal block data and enable the transfer of information about unknown correlators between paired theories. We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior, with approximation accuracy depending on architecture, regulator, and parameter distribution. These results connect the exact mathematical structure of conformal field theory with the expressive and computational properties of neural field theories.

title_en: Projection-Based Partitioned MiLAC Architecture for MU-MIMO Precoding
abstract_en: This work proposes a partitioned Microwave Linear Analog Computer (MiLAC) architecture for user-specific MU-MIMO precoding based on independently configured analog subnetworks. The proposed method reformulates user-level interference suppression as an invertible projection-based transformation, which is computed from the channel and synthesized into the MiLAC admittances. While the resulting offline configuration incurs higher computational complexity than conventional ZFBF and regularized ZFBF, it remains substantially below fully digital Block Diagonalization. Once configured, the Sub-MiLACs perform the precoding operation in the analog domain, yielding significantly lower online processing complexity. Under ideal conditions, the proposed method achieves performance close to fully digital BD.

title_en: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
abstract_en: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $Ω(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. Broadcast simulations match analytic averages at $N=1024$, without resolved bias growth up to $N=2^{20}$. Fault-tolerant hardware, gate rates and, in continuous broadcast, report counts remain open.

title_en: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
abstract_en: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

title_en: Beyond Bilingual: Studying Quadrilingual Code-Switching with Conversational AI
abstract_en: Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.

title_en: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels
abstract_en: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. In earlier work, about two hundred labels and a TF-IDF logistic regression had the highest point accuracy on this inbox, though not significantly above the best hosted model; we ask whether the same labels, given to a decision model, close the gap. A first registered study, on a generic 4B base with cross-validation and message type only, stayed below the baseline at every label budget (-1.8 to -7.3 points). The main study was registered before any fine-tuning run: a fixed test set of 135 emails never used for selection, LoRA adapters on the public Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B decision models, nested subsets of 50 to 587 labels, two seeds and five decision fields on a free T4 GPU. Four of its five hypotheses are refuted--two in the fine-tunes' favour--and one is confirmed for one model. On message type the 4B model misses the registered three-point margin at 400 labels (+2.6) and passes it with all 587 (+3.3); with all labels both models are above the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points, where one email is 0.74 points and a 95% interval is about 15 points wide, and the 4B model is clearly ahead in type macro-F1 (0.581 vs. 0.406). On the three action switches the baseline is ahead at every label budget for both models (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899 mean accuracy with all labels), at under a millisecond per question against 306 and 1681 ms. The 0.8B type curve barely improves after 300 labels and then falls. The baseline never predicts the two rarest classes (7 offers and 8 spam in the training pool); the fine-tuned models find spam in some runs, not consistently across seeds. We list the explanations we did not test and say when a new attempt would be worth making. Scripts are public; weights and emails are not.

title_en: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models
abstract_en: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-δ$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.

title_en: What You Post Is What You Symptom: Estimating Psychometric Networks from Social Media Discourse
abstract_en: Symptom networks in psychopathology are estimated almost exclusively from self-report questionnaires, restricting inference to whatever symptom set a given instrument covers. We introduce a framework for symptom-resolved network estimation directly from social media discourse and apply the framework to depression and eating disorders, with a third anorexia corpus as cross-dataset validation. To our knowledge, we are the first to estimate symptom-resolved psychometric networks from social media text, compare them to clinical co-endorsement networks, and replicate transdiagnostic linguistic markers across 3 independently recruited corpora spanning 2 disorders simultaneously. For depression, expression scores correlate with BDI-II totals at $ρ{=}0.434$, 20 of 21 items reach FDR significance, and split-half reliability is 0.935. The Network Comparison Test detects few edge differences between modalities (3-5\% of edges), while bridge symptoms diverge. For eating disorders, the item-level results are exploratory. Identified linguistic features replicate the same direction across all 3 corpora, and they cluster in three construct families.

title_en: Differentiable Exact Learning
abstract_en: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.

title_en: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
abstract_en: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

title_en: Expertise capture in workplace AI
abstract_en: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.

title_en: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
abstract_en: Large language models are increasingly exposed to model-generated text, raising the possibility that future models will be trained recursively on the outputs of their predecessors. Prior work on such self-consuming training loops has largely focused on output quality and downstream performance, leaving their effects on internal representations poorly understood. We study how representations evolve across five generations of self-consumption and whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) remain reliable under this shift. At each generation, we compare a lineage trained on synthetic data with a matched control trained on real data under the same training settings. We evaluate how well SAEs trained before self-consumption transfer to later generations, measuring reconstruction and sparsity across SAE widths, architectures, and model layers. We then fine-tune the original SAE on each generation and use sparse probing to test whether task-relevant information remains concentrated in a small number of latents or becomes more distributed across the representation. We find that zero-shot SAE performance degrades progressively under self-consumption, with growing reconstruction and sparsity gaps that vary substantially across layers. Fine-tuning largely restores reconstruction, but not feature-level usefulness: task-relevant information remains accessible in the full latent space while becoming less concentrated in individual features. These results show that self-consumption induces representational drift and that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to establish that an adapted SAE remains equally useful for interpretation.

title_en: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
abstract_en: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

title_en: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning
abstract_en: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. We show that self-attention is a real-space Dyson iteration whose Boltzmann (softmax) kernel acts as a two-body self-energy. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, Löwdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.

title_en: Federated TD Learning in Heterogeneous Environments with Average Rewards: A Two-timescale Approach with Polyak-Ruppert Averaging
abstract_en: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a promising way to speedup training in reinforcement learning when one has access to multiple edge devices that can operate in parallel. Recently, it has been shown that even when these edge devices have access to different dynamic models---such as cars or robots with differing system configurations---an optimal convergence rate that has a linear speedup proportional to the number of devices is achievable. However, this result requires that the algorithm's stepsize be chosen in a manner that depends on the unknown model parameters. Also, it applies only to a discounted setting, which has been argued to fit episodic tasks better than continuing control tasks. In this paper, we obtain finite-time bounds for heterogeneous FRL with average rewards. We show that optimal convergence rate and linear speedup are achievable even with a universal stepsize choice, independent of the underlying dynamics. To achieve our result, we modify the existing one-timescale FRL method to a novel two-timescale variant that additionally incorporates iterate averaging. We remark that this idea also extends to other settings already studied in the literature, such as the homogeneous FRL or the heterogeneous case with a discounted cost function.

title_en: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models
abstract_en: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

title_en: TEMPO: Regime-Aware Operator Learning with Locally Adapted POD Bases
abstract_en: Operator learning approximates the solution map of a parametric partial differential equation from data, enabling fast prediction at new parameter values without repeated simulation. The dominant approach fits a single global low-rank basis, typically a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), to all solution snapshots. This fails when the snapshots span qualitatively different solution shapes, from smooth diffusive profiles to near-discontinuous shocks. We propose TEMPO (Trajectory Expectation-Maximization Mixture of POD Operators), a two-phase framework for regime-aware operator learning. In the offline phase, TEMPO recovers latent regimes via expectation-maximization, fitting a dedicated linear or nonlinear basis to each discovered regime. In the online phase, a gating network and per-regime branch networks are trained jointly, routing new inputs to the regimes at inference. We test TEMPO on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow and the heterogeneous Helmholtz equation. With 64 total POD modes, TEMPO gives 18.61% test error on Burgers', compared with 19.61% for global POD. It also gives lower errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.

title_en: Anchoring Motion, Refining Trajectories: Generalizable Continuous Neural Decoding
abstract_en: Brain activity encodes motor information across multiple temporal scales, enabling continuous neural control beyond discrete action recognition. However, existing methods are typically tailored to specific subjects and tasks, with direct neural-to-kinematic mappings that can entangle subject-specific neural variability with task-dependent motion patterns, limiting generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce AMRT, a shared neural decoding framework for heterogeneous electrode configurations and movement paradigms. Motivated by cortical encoding of movement direction and speed, AMRT adopts a two-stage design that anchors local motion through velocity estimation and refines the resulting trajectories over longer horizons, encouraging reuse of local motion tendencies across subjects and tasks. Across three datasets, AMRT generalizes to unseen trials and subjects and demonstrates transfer potential across neural recordings and movement paradigms, highlighting the potential of shared neural representations and anchor-and-refine decoding for generalizable continuous neural control.

title_en: Nonparametric Instrumental Kernel Regression: The Well- and Misspecified Setting Under General Link Conditions
abstract_en: We study nonparametric instrumental variable regression when the outcome takes values in a separable Hilbert space $\mathbb{Y}$, for instance a curve, a density or the kernel mean embedding of a distribution. The structural function solves an ill-posed operator equation whose conditional expectation operator need not be injective, and whose solutions need not belong to the hypothesis space. We analyse a two-stage kernel estimator that extends kernel instrumental variable regression to $\mathbb{Y}$-valued outcomes and allows spectral regularisation in both stages, including Landweber iteration and Showalter's method in the second stage. We show that the second stage is a regularisation method in the Hilbert scale generated by the inverse of the kernel integral operator. This viewpoint identifies the solution towards which the estimator converges: the minimum-norm solution in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space in the well-specified case and, in the misspecified case, the unique solution in the range of the continuous extension of the projection operator associated to the well-specified setting. Under source conditions and link conditions expressed through general index functions, we derive non-asymptotic bounds in a scale of interpolation norms that hold with high probability in terms of the first-stage error, with or without identification and in the well- and misspecified settings. For polynomial link conditions, we recover the rate of scalar kernel instrumental regression and extend it to targets outside the hypothesis space; for exponential link conditions, we obtain logarithmic rates in the severely ill-posed regime.

title_en: Quality and Similarity Indicators for Video-Based Heart Rate and Respiratory Rate Fusion: A Controlled Evaluation
abstract_en: Camera-based heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR) estimates vary in reliability from window to window, and a common remedy is to fuse several extraction methods with weights from reference-free signal quality indicators. However, few studies test whether these indicators identify the most accurate method in each window or outperform simpler fusion. We evaluate 11 quality indicators and 8 inter-method similarity measures for fusing 7 HR and 10 RR extractors on four public datasets (75 test subjects). Filters, indicator directions, weighting parameters and a learned ridge baseline are selected on a separate five-subject set before testing. Fusion is compared with equal averaging, a constant typical-rate predictor, the best single method selected in advance and in hindsight, and a per-window oracle with a permutation-based null, using subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals. For HR, quality-weighted fusion reduced mean absolute error by 10.9% [5.2, 18.4] relative to averaging and by 15.6% [8.1, 23.1] relative to the method selected in advance, and was statistically indistinguishable from the best method selected in hindsight. Weighting methods by their agreement did not improve on averaging. For RR, the indicators could not identify the more accurate estimates: sharpened quality weighting increased error (-2.6% [-4.8, -0.8]), fused estimates were uncorrelated with the reference (r <= 0.22), and averaging was less accurate than the typical-rate predictor (-3.1% [-6.1, -0.4]). With a second respiratory reference, apparent RR gains reflected estimates moving toward its typical rate. Quality-guided fusion is worthwhile for video HR; for RR, 30-s windows improved estimates but not fusion.

title_en: Portrait Fitness as a Pretext: Probing Implicit Demographic Bias in VLMs
abstract_en: We audit face-related bias in VLMs using BALPORTRAITS, a new balanced dataset of 9,000 fictional portraits across ethnicity, gender, and age segments. Sixteen VLMs estimate portrait fitness scores for occupations, brands, activities, and banking or insurance products within an advertising-casting framework designed to avoid direct inference of protected attributes. Item-level estimations are aggregated with scenario-specific prestige scores to compare rankings across demographic groups. While the magnitude and direction of these biases vary across scenarios, model families, and demographic dimensions, with age, ethnicity, and gender contributing differently depending on the task, we find demographic dispersion across all evaluated models, with a majority of pairwise segment differences reaching statistical significance. This study introduces a controlled protocol to assess implicit face-related associations and demonstrates that single-scenario or single-attribute audits are insufficient.

title_en: Location Privacy for ISAC Systems: Rate, Sensing, and Privacy Tradeoff
abstract_en: In this paper, we design a beamformer for transmitter location privacy in an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system, where the transmitter communicates with a receiver while sensing a point target. We adopt the direction-of-arrival obfuscation power ratio (DoA-OPR), the ratio of the received power in a prescribed fake direction to that in the actual direction, as the location privacy metric. To design the beamformer, we formulate an achievable rate maximization problem subject to constraints on total transmit power, target sensing, location privacy, and the number of data streams. The resulting problem is nonconvex and is addressed through an eigenmode-selection and power-allocation framework. To reduce the computational complexity of the solution, we develop strategies that eliminate infeasible candidate solutions. Furthermore, we propose a fake angle selection technique in which the transmit power for target sensing aids location privacy. Numerical results illustrate the achievable rate-sensing-privacy tradeoff and show that the proposed fake angle selection technique performs better than the random fake angle selection technique.

title_en: Quantum Optimization Algorithm for Pinching-Antenna Activation with Max-Min Fairness
abstract_en: In this letter, we propose a training-free quantum approximate optimization algorithm with a linear-ramp schedule (LR-QAOA) for antenna activation in pinching-antenna systems (PASS). Since all active pinching antennas (PAs) share one feed and split its power, maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the weakest user becomes a combinatorial max-min problem that must be re-solved whenever the users move. We formulate the problem as a two-local Ising Hamiltonian with one qubit per PA and no penalty terms, employing a weightedsum surrogate to prioritize weaker users. Instead of training the circuit with a classical optimizer, the proposed LR-QAOA method tunes its parameters via a linear ramp; the measured patterns are ranked by the exact max-min objective, and the best ones are refined with a short local search using the same number of evaluated patterns. Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed LR-QAOA method outperforms greedy activation, projection-guided activation, and semidefinite relaxation-based classical baseline methods when all methods test the same number of PA on/off patterns. Experiments on real IBM Quantum hardware further show that the execution time remains nearly constant as the number of PAs grows, whereas exhaustive search grows exponentially. However, gate noise in the NISQ era restricts near-optimal hardware solutions to small numbers of antennas only.

title_en: From very fine Vertical Resolution to Range Super-Resolution on BIOMASS P-BAND SAR Data
abstract_en: This paper demonstrates range super-resolution over arid regions using SAR tomography data with very fine vertical resolution from the European Space Agency's BIOMASS mission. As the first civilian spaceborne P-band SAR mission, BIOMASS is operating with a bandwidth limited to 6~MHz by International Telecommunication Union regulations, yielding a native slant-range resolution of approximately 25 m. The large spatial baseline data acquired during the commissioning phase in July and August 2025 provide a valuable opportunity to enhance range resolution based on the InSAR wavenumber shift principle. According to this principle, a wider effective bandwidth can be synthesized by combining complementary sub-bands of the ground reflectivity spectrum sampled across acquisitions at different look angles. Unlike existing literature, this paper offers a novel interpretation of this problem from the perspective of SAR tomography. Furthermore, the proposed method also accounts for residual topography errors. The range resolution enhancement performance is validated using all 20 available acquisitions from the July-August 2025 commissioning phase over Lop Nur, China, and Wadi al-Hayat, Libya, achieving spatial detail comparable to optical satellite imagery in a grid finer than 2 m. Furthermore, the reconstructed range spectrum of the central Libyan oasis exhibits an effective bandwidth exceeding 70 MHz. The point spread function (PSF) of a point like target in the scene demonstrates a slant-range resolution finer than 2.1 m, representing more than a twelvefold improvement over the native resolution.

title_en: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
abstract_en: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

title_en: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
abstract_en: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

title_en: Teaching Language Models to Adapt Answer Granularity to Their Confidence
abstract_en: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

title_en: Verifiable Random Sampling of Private Data Without a Trusted Single Party
abstract_en: Problem: When a party supports claims about a private dataset by disclosing a sample, auditors cannot tell whether it was drawn at random or "cherry-picked" to hide flaws in the rest of the data. Solution: The data holder commits to the hashes of every item in its dataset and registers the commitment with independent servers. Selection then waits on a decentralized randomness beacon: a network that jointly emits a fresh random value every few seconds, outside the control of the data holder and the auditors. The value emitted two beacon rounds after the commitment picks the sample. Each server returns a signed receipt, so anyone can later check that the revealed sample is exactly the one that value prescribes. Selection from the committed set stays unbiased as long as the beacon's threshold holds and one required server is honest, and a pre-agreed name, checked with the servers, stops repeated or abandoned draws. We call this protocol NoCherry. Applications: Any audit that spot-checks a private corpus: private AI benchmarks and held-out test sets, dataset quality claims, code and security audits, test-fairness review, vulnerability handling, and compliance sampling. Auditors need not trust the data holder to hand over a representative sample of the committed data, since the protocol proves it, and data holders need not expose their entire dataset.

title_en: Wavelet-Energy-Driven Dynamic Patching for Time Series Forecasting
abstract_en: Patch-based transformers tokenise a time series into fixed-size, uniform windows, which commits the model to a single temporal resolution even though real signals are multi-scale. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) is a natural alternative because it decomposes a signal across scales. A growing body of work makes the wavelet filter learnable, on the assumption that a more flexible wavelet forecasts better. That assumption has rarely been tested in isolation, because a single reported improvement usually credits three things at once. These are the use of any multi-resolution decomposition, the choice of wavelet and training the filter. We introduce a forecaster that turns a learnable-DWT per-scale energy map into variable-length patches by merging adjacent windows that share a dominant scale. Three findings follow. First, most of the improvement is there before any filter is learned. A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on eight of the nine datasets by 1.5% to 7.8%, and on four of them it recovers all of the gain. Traffic is the one exception, where it is 1.2% worse. Second, learning the filter gives a further improvement on only some datasets. It helps on three of the nine datasets and makes Traffic 2.7% worse. Third, having variable-length patches helps, but exactly where their boundaries fall does not. A fixed-size uniform grid, even with its patch size tuned per task, is worse than our variable-length patches on 27 of 36 settings. Recomputing the boundaries from the learned filter at every step, rather than caching them once, never helps. The improvement in wavelet-based forecasting comes from the multi-resolution structure and the variable-length patches it induces, not from making the wavelet learnable. In practice, start from any valid wavelet, cache the patch boundaries once and treat training the filter as a per-dataset decision rather than a default.

title_en: High-probability Uniform Mixing via Dobrushin Contraction and Accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
abstract_en: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, since its invention and subsequent rise to widespread use, has been motivated by its ability to accelerate convergence to equilibrium compared to diffusive methods, both in terms of dependence on condition number and dimension. In the present work, we establish this acceleration simultaneously in both aspects for critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms. More precisely, for target measures $μ(dx)\propto e^{-U(x)}dx$ with $m$-strongly convex, $L$-gradient Lipschitz, and $L_H$-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, we show that the method mixes to $\varepsilon$-accuracy in total variation using $\mathcal O\bigl((κ^{1/2}+L_H^{1/2}m^{-3/4})\,d^{1/4}\bigr)$ gradient evaluations up to logarithmic factors, both uniformly over starting points in domains of high equilibrium probability and from warm starts. The proof incorporates ideas from previous studies by Bou-Rabee and Chen et al. that show either aspect of acceleration separately, into novel coupling technology. This new coupling technology for general Markov chains extends earlier frameworks aimed at capturing fast local equilibration in the presence of slow global mixing. Specifically, via a weak-$(1,1)$ maximal inequality that follows from Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem, we uncover a stability mechanism in high-probability domains with respect to equilibrium. This enables straightforward localization to naturally arising domains of fast local mixing, and seamlessly fits broad local frameworks via Dobrushin contraction, Wasserstein contraction and local Harris' theorems. We develop the Dobrushin formulation.

title_en: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
abstract_en: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

title_en: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning for Sample Efficient Experimentation
abstract_en: Self-driving laboratories must learn to control a process from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, too few for deep reinforcement learning (RL). We learn the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process (GP), which avoids learning the dynamics, and show that the GP posterior supplies the learning rate of Q-learning. If each Bellman target is treated as a noisy measurement of the Q-function, the learning rate that minimises the mean squared error is the Kalman gain, and applying it to every observed transition is equivalent to GP regression. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ) sets the noise variance of each target with a heteroscedastic GP, which learns how unreliable the targets are across the states and inputs. Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

title_en: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
abstract_en: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

title_en: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
abstract_en: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.

title_en: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
abstract_en: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

title_en: Dimension-free spectral laws and the risk of spectral filters
abstract_en: Spectral properties of the sample covariance are key to modern machine learning with high-dimensional data. Random matrix theory (RMT) supplies powerful tools; however, most classical results assume proportional asymptotics, where $d/n$ tends to a finite limit. In functional data analysis and kernel methods, a fixed infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is often the more natural setting for the observations, beyond the scope of proportional asymptotics. This calls for a dimension-free spectral theory for i.i.d. observations $\boldsymbol{x}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{x}_n$ in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ with trace-class population covariance $Σ$. Building on the dimension-free ridge regression analysis of Cheng and Montanari (2024), we establish two deterministic equivalents with explicit nonasymptotic error bounds. The first approximates the empirical spectral law $\widehatμ_n$ of the sample Gram matrix by a deterministic law $μ_n$. The second characterizes the conditional prediction risk of analytic spectral filters in linear regression. Previous sharp approximations to prediction risk in this setting have focused on ridge regression and closely-related problems. Our analysis covers a broader class of filters at the bulk scale, with an explicit user-friendly spectral stability condition to check. We apply our theory to power and critical spectral laws, and we recover the proportional regime. For prediction, we study (negative) ridge estimators, iterated ridge, and gradient flow. Mathematically, building on the idea of stochastic interpolation, we construct a deterministic backward path to interpolate the spectral parameter. The resulting bounds on resolvent and mixed-resolvent traces give mesoscopic approximations to the spectral law within the bulk and, by Cauchy's formula, deterministic equivalents for the prediction variance and squared bias of analytic spectral filters.

title_en: A Study on Performance Enhancement of a Webcam-Based Real-Time Eye-Tracking System
abstract_en: This study proposes a real-time gaze-tracking system that uses a standard RGB webcam to estimate screen coordinates. The system combines ETH-XGaze-based gaze estimation with nine-point calibration and polynomial ridge regression. To reduce errors caused by changes in head position, it also applies a conditional residual correction derived from head and pose features extracted with RTMPose. Whether this correction is used depends on the reliability of the detected features and the characteristics of the calibration data. In a preliminary experiment, one participant completed trials at 12 screen targets. The resulting mean screen-coordinate error was 204.24 pixels, which was 35.83% lower than that of xgaze-js and 57.69% lower than that of gaze_tracker. The system produced valid gaze estimates for all 12 targets. These preliminary findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining user-specific calibration with conditional pose-based correction for webcam gaze tracking. Because the evaluation involved only one participant, further experiments with more participants and a wider range of postures are required.

title_en: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
abstract_en: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. title_en: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
abstract_en: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

title_en: What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds
abstract_en: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

title_en: Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration
abstract_en: Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.

title_en: Towards wearable-scale, transition-aware sleep staging for clinical populations
abstract_en: Automatic sleep staging models are predominantly developed on healthy sleepers and generalize poorly to clinical populations with fragmented sleep. Across three cohorts (patients with stroke, isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder, and other sleep disorders), we observe 2-3x more awakenings per hour, nearly twice as much N1, and less REM sleep than in healthy sleepers. In patient-wise 10-fold cross-validation, Gcv-TAD improves per-patient macro F1 over supervised training on the same labels by +3.2 to +7.6 points on average. title_en: When Feature Representation Changes Local Explanations: A Controlled Comparison of SHAP and LIME under Numerical Discretization
abstract_en: Local feature attributions are computed over a feature representation chosen by an upstream data-engineering step, yet they are read as statements about the underlying quantity. We ask how discretizing one continuous feature changes local KernelSHAP and LIME explanations when the classifier is held fixed, and whether the two explainers respond differently. A random forest is trained on UCI Adult and frozen; age is collapsed onto equi-width or quantile bin representatives (k in {3,5,10}) before the model receives it, and the same 120 held-out instances are explained in every condition across multiple seeds. We show analytically and numerically that for KernelSHAP this is exactly equivalent to explaining the unchanged model at the quantized instance against a quantized background, so the comparison is between two effective inputs rather than a pure explainer effect; for LIME no such equivalence holds. Each attribution change is compared with a seed-noise floor from re-running the explainer on the unchanged condition. KernelSHAP's age attribution exceeds its noise floor in all 6 pre-specified conditions (median ratios 2.4-59, all significant after Holm correction); on the raw scale LIME's exceeds its floor in only 2 of 6 and in the rest is no larger than its own run-to-run variation. SHAP's normalized change exceeds LIME's in every condition (rank-biserial 0.81-1.00), while LIME is 2.5-4.6x less consistent across repeats. Predicted classes change for only 0.8-5.8% of instances and held-out ROC-AUC never falls below 0.9097, yet 45-94% of instances show a large SHAP attribution change with no class flip. Feature-importance rankings barely move (median Spearman >= 0.979, top-3 overlap 1.00). The representation change and the change in effective input cannot be separated within a frozen-model design.

title_en: Cap-Aware Boosting for Green Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting
abstract_en: Accurate forecasting of Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM) electricity prices is essential for market participants in the Indian power sector. We present a LightGBM-based forecasting framework for Indian Energy Exchange GDAM prices, which clear in 96 fifteen-minute intervals per day. The proposed system explicitly models price-cap behavior by separating capped-price events from normal market conditions. A classification head estimates the probability of the regulatory price cap (Rs 10,000/MWh), while a regression head predicts uncapped prices in logarithmic space. Final forecasts are obtained through probabilistic blending of these components and are accompanied by nine quantile forecasts for uncertainty estimation. Evaluated on 257 trading days between 1 January and 14 September 2026, the model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 397.9 Rs/MWh and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 9.57%, substantially outperforming a Chronos-2 baseline (583.3 MAE) and a persistence baseline using the previous day's profile (589.1 MAE). We further introduce leak-safe variants that incorporate real-time market signals, unmatched sell volumes, and solar generation proxies. In a recent out-of-sample evaluation, the quantile-clock variant achieved the best short-term performance with an MAE of 789 Rs/MWh during 25-28 October, while the enhanced capped-price model achieved an MAE of 716 Rs/MWh across 21 evaluation days through 16 November. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of regime-aware probabilistic forecasting for high-volatility electricity markets.

title_en: Summary Sufficiency in Simulation-Based Inference via Mutual Information
abstract_en: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods typically rely on low-dimensional summary statistics as conditioning inputs for posterior estimation, making their sufficiency crucial for accurate inference. Mutual information (MI) provides a natural information-theoretic characterization of sufficiency, quantifying how much parameter information a summary retains. However, these MI quantities are generally intractable in likelihood-free settings. Sui et al. (2026) estimate MI from a trained neural posterior using the Barber--Agakov (BA) lower bound, while discussing, but not computing, a Fisher-information upper bound. This makes the estimate ambiguous: a small lower bound may indicate either an insufficient summary or an inaccurate density estimator. We address this limitation with a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and reveals what the difference between bounds has actually measured. We extend the resulting sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces, allowing simulations to focus on a neighborhood of the data while preserving the target posterior and enabling valid sufficiency comparisons between summaries. We illustrate the use of this diagnostic tool on a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model by comparing learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.

title_en: DRaGAN: Dynamic Graph Attention Network for Multi-Radar Point Cloud Encoding in Automotive Radar Perception
abstract_en: Radar represents a key modality for weather-robust perception. Unlike optical sensors such as camera and LiDAR, radar can penetrate fog, rain and snow due to its longer wavelength, and recent hardware advances have steadily improved its spatial resolution, thus making it increasingly relevant for autonomous systems. While processing raw radar data requires substantial memory computation, most existing work has focused on preprocessed point-cloud data similar to LiDAR. However, the sparse radar points and sensor-relative anisotropy make LiDAR-oriented encoders suboptimal. To address this problem, we present DRaGAN, a dynamic graph attention network for multi-radar point clouds. DRaGAN introduces a sensor-relative Fourier encoding of angle and range to capture fixed-aperture radar characteristics, gated short- and long-range hub nodes along each sensor's line of sight for efficient local-global message passing, and attention-guided dynamic rewiring that prunes weak edges and adds a bounded number of latent connections restricted to two-hop neighborhoods. This reduces the number of processed edges in deeper layers while preserving representation quality. On TruckScenes, DRaGAN improves test NDS by 10.10 points over the evaluated RadarGNN baseline and reduces the reported model FLOP count by 63.7%. This trade-off includes an increase in model latency from 40 to 53.16 ms and in trainable parameters from 1.2M to 1.7M on the evaluated implementations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/chr-is-tof/DRaGAN.

title_en: Dataset Distillation for Handwritten Text Recognition: An Empirical Study
abstract_en: Dataset distillation (DD) replaces large training datasets with smaller synthetic ones to reduce computational costs. While traditionally used for classification, we present, to our knowledge, the first DD study for line-level handwritten text recognition (HTR). Unlike classification tasks, which use discrete labels, HTR employs unaligned sequences from a virtually infinite output space as labels. To adapt classification-based DD methods to this scenario, we define text pseudo-classes by clustering transcriptions based on character n-grams. We adapt gradient matching (GM), distribution matching (DM) and trajectory matching (MTT) to a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC). In this process, synthetic line images are generated by optimising only the pixels of real starting lines (either randomly chosen or selected as text medoids), while keeping their original transcriptions fixed. Across four datasets (IAM, George Washington, READ\,2016, LAM) and three budgets (1--10\,\% of the training lines), no distilled set outperforms its real initialisation lines. Random lines prove better than medoids, and further optimisation only degrades recognition. Methodologically, DM lowers its objective without benefit, while GM and MTT barely move theirs. We turn these findings into guidelines for evaluating data compression in HTR.
